Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you turn this into a clear prompt for explaining and reviewing the sql below? i'm helping the morning team at North Quay depot understand a delivery summary that someone copied into a draft handover note. The note is meant to help the shift lead compare incoming volume across depots, but the only thing i have to work from is this query. Please base the explanation and review on the snippet itself, not on assumptions about our database, dashboard, or warehouse process. don't run it or pretend we have results; i need a request that asks someone to explain what the code says and what it leaves open.

The handover is being assembled for a Monday meeting, and the team has asked whether the query is intended to describe a particular week. I can't see a date field or a date condition in the code, so please make that a point to check rather than quietly treating it as a weekly total. A driver called Lina said, “I thought received units meant everything unloaded at the gate.” The shift lead, Omar, replied, “Maybe, but I want to know what this query actually counts before we put that in the note.” Those are their comments, not definitions of the fields. Keep the explanation grounded in the code and don't choose between their interpretations unless the snippet supports it.

Here is the complete snippet as it was sent to me. It has four lines, and the last line matters because it shows how the rows are grouped. Please keep the supplied lines together in the prompt, so the person reviewing it can see the entire query rather than being told to find it elsewhere.

SELECT depot_id, SUM(units) AS received_units
FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'received' AND units > 42
GROUP BY depot_id;

I am asking for an explanation that a depot shift lead can follow without assuming they already know SQL. Cover what table the query names, which fields appear in its output, what the SUM is doing, and what the alias received_units labels. Explain the filter carefully: there are two conditions joined in the WHERE clause, and both must be true for a row to be included. In particular, help the reviewer distinguish the status check from the numeric units check. Don't turn this into a claim about total units from every delivery, because the query has a threshold and a status filter. The team is trying to read the code accurately, not to make a general statement about depot activity.

Please also review the sequence of operations in ordinary language, especially how rows that pass the filter are collected by depot_id and how the displayed sum relates to that grouping. If the code does not tell us what a depot identifier means, whether units are cases or individual items, or what period the table covers, say those details are not established here. We use printed depot labels on the loading board, but I don't know whether those labels correspond exactly to depot_id, so don't equate them. No schema, sample records, or report definition was provided with the snippet. Keep those gaps separate from things the query does state.

For the review, call out questions that follow directly from the text of the query rather than proposing a replacement. For example, ask whether leaving out rows with units of 42 or less is intended, and whether the status spelling in the filter matches the values used in the deliveries table; the code alone doesn't confirm either business choice. You can mention that the condition is strictly greater than 42, not greater than or equal to 42. Don't claim that the chosen threshold is wrong or right. If the explanation cannot establish what the business team means by received, mark that as something to confirm instead of supplying a definition.

A small test section would be useful, but it should describe cases to check, not provide fabricated output. Include a row whose status is received and whose units are above 42, a row with another status, and a received row at exactly 42. Also ask what happens when qualifying rows share a depot_id, since that is relevant to the grouping and sum. Avoid assigning example depots, counts, or totals that are not in the code. If the reviewer cannot determine expected results without table contents, say so; the request is to identify useful checks, not to invent records or run the query.

There is a second note from the coordinator, Priya: “Please keep the handover plain enough to read aloud, but don't hide the filter.” That should shape the requested explanation without changing its meaning. The reviewer can use brief headings and concise language, but should distinguish what is explicit from what would need confirmation. If this turns out to be included in the Monday weekly discussion, flag that the snippet itself has no visible date range; do not silently call it a weekly summary. At the same time, don't make the absence of a date condition into a claim that the query was not used for a week. We only know what appears in these four lines.

Please organize the eventual explanation, review, and suggested checks around the query as supplied. Keep the scope to explaining and assessing this snippet for the handover, using only the code and the limited context above. Don't execute it, add columns or conditions, rewrite the SQL, assert what the database contains, or give a final operational conclusion. The useful end point is a clear account of what can be read from the code, the questions it raises, and the checks a reviewer could make if the needed data or definitions become available.
